title: Recursion Patterns
summary: **Recursion** solves a problem by answering a small case directly and asking the same **function** to solve a smaller version.
refresher: A recursive **function** needs a **base case** and a smaller **recursive call**. The base case stops the calls. The smaller call moves the input toward that stop point.
refresher_code:
if done: return answer
return work + solve(smaller_input)

advanced-recursion-base-case.title: The base case stops recursion
advanced-recursion-base-case.body: A **base case** is the simple answer the **function** can **return** immediately.
advanced-recursion-base-case.notice: Without a reachable **base case**, **recursion** keeps calling itself.
advanced-recursion-base-case.mistake: A **base case** that never runs is the same as no base case.

advanced-recursion-shrink.title: Each call must get smaller
advanced-recursion-shrink.body: The **recursive call** should move closer to the **base case**.

sections.title: Base case first
sections.summary: The **base case** is the stop sign.

blocks.body: **Recursion** is a **function** calling itself. The pattern is simple: stop when the answer is obvious, otherwise solve a smaller version and use that answer.

blocks.title: Follow the call stack
blocks.caption: Watch calls pile up until the **base case**, then **return** back down.

steps.title: Call fact(3)
steps.body: The first call cannot answer yet. It needs fact(2).

steps.title: Call fact(2)
steps.body: fact(2) also needs a smaller answer.

steps.title: Call fact(1)
steps.body: fact(1) is the **base case**, so it can answer immediately.

steps.title: Return upward
steps.body: Now each waiting call can finish using the smaller answer.

steps.title: Finish
steps.body: fact(3) uses fact(2)'s result and returns 6.

blocks.caption: Factorial has an obvious stop at 0.

blocks.title: Read it line by line
items: Otherwise, multiply `n` by the answer for `n - 1`.
`n - 1` is closer to 0, so the calls eventually stop.
Each unfinished call waits for the smaller call to **return**.

blocks.title: Same input means stuck
blocks.body: `factorial(n)` inside `factorial` calls the same problem again. Nothing gets smaller, so it cannot naturally stop.

blocks.prompt: What is the job of the **base case**?
choices: Stop the recursion with a direct answer
blocks.why: The **base case** gives the **function** a place to stop.

sections.title: Make the problem smaller
sections.summary: The **recursive call** should move toward the **base case**.

blocks.body: A **recursive call** should solve the same kind of problem with less **input**: one smaller number, the rest of a **list**, or a child node in a tree.

blocks.title: Return values come back up
blocks.caption: Watch `sum_list([2, 4, 6])` wait for smaller calls, then add results on the way back.

steps.title: Ask for the full sum
steps.body: The first call keeps 2 and asks for the sum of the rest.
steps.what_changed: The **call stack** stores the unfinished work: 2 plus a smaller answer.

steps.title: Ask again
steps.body: The next call keeps 4 and asks for the sum of [6].
steps.what_changed: Each call is the same job with a smaller **list**.

steps.title: Hit the empty list
steps.what_changed: Now the waiting calls can finally finish.

steps.title: Add back up
steps.what_changed: **Return** values move back to the calls that were waiting for them.

steps.title: Finish
steps.body: The first call returns 2 + 10, which is 12.
steps.what_changed: The **stack** is done because every smaller answer returned.

blocks.caption: Sum a **list** by taking the first item and asking **recursion** to sum the rest.

blocks.title: Trace `sum_list([2, 4, 6])`
items: The empty **list** returns 0, then the waiting calls add back up to 12.

blocks.prompt: Where do unfinished recursive calls wait?
blocks.why: The **call stack** remembers each unfinished **function** call until its smaller call returns.

sections.title: Unwind and combine answers
sections.summary: Small answers return first, then waiting calls combine them.

blocks.body: A recursive **function** has a forward trip and a return trip. The forward trip makes smaller calls. The return trip **unwinds** those calls and combines the returned values.

blocks.title: Watch recursive calls unwind
blocks.caption: The smallest call returns first, then each waiting call finishes.

steps.title: Call with 3
steps.body: The function is not at the base case yet, so it asks for the answer to a smaller input.

steps.title: Unwind answers
steps.body: Each waiting call combines its number with the returned smaller answer.

blocks.prompt: What happens after the base case returns?
choices: waiting calls finish in reverse order
all calls restart from the beginning
blocks.why: The most recent waiting call resumes first, then earlier calls finish one by one.

sections.title: Recursion fits trees
sections.summary: A **tree** problem often repeats on left and right children.

blocks.body: Tree **recursion** works because each child is the **root** of a smaller tree. A height **function** can ask for the height of the left subtree and the right subtree, then combine them.

blocks.title: Name what comes back
blocks.body: A recursive **function** should have a clear **return** meaning. Here, `height(node)` means the height of the **tree** starting at `node`.

sections.title: When recursion can be slow
sections.summary: Some recursive solutions are clear but repeat work.

blocks.body: **Recursion** is not automatically efficient. Naive Fibonacci is the common warning because it recalculates the same **values** many times.

blocks.caption: Repeated work can grow quickly.
blocks.wrong:
fib(n) = fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)
// repeats many calls
blocks.right:
store earlier answers or use a loop
// each answer is computed once
blocks.body: The idea is not that **recursion** is bad. The idea is to notice repeated work.

blocks.prompt: Why can naive recursive Fibonacci be slow?
choices: It repeats the same subproblems many times
blocks.why: The same Fibonacci **values** are recomputed again and again.
